title: What Part of a Grade Belongs to the Student
author: Terry Yu
summary: Terry Yu interrogates what a letter grade actually measures, distinguishing between what students bring to the classroom versus what teachers contribute to their learning. Drawing on Value-Added Measurement (VAM) and the Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) project, Yu argues that students arrive with a pre-existing grade trajectory shaped by prior test scores, socioeconomic context, habits of mind, and self-efficacy beliefs. Teacher value is defined as the shift in trajectory beyond what prior inputs predicted. The article critiques grade inflation strategies like Harvard-style caps and argues that grading is a complex, classroom-level question that cannot be answered from aggregate data. The central insight is that most variance in student learning arrives on day one carried by the student, and teacher contribution is the change above that baseline.
points: Every student enters a classroom with a probabilistic grade trajectory already shaped by prior test scores, socioeconomic context, motivational orientations, and self-efficacy beliefs -- making grading inherently a measurement of change, not just performance level.

The MET project, the most rigorous large-scale teaching effectiveness study in US K-12 education, built its methodology on one uncomfortable premise: without controlling for what students bring, any measure of teacher effectiveness is confounded from the start.

Self-efficacy beliefs -- a student's conviction about their capacity to succeed -- are among the strongest predictors of academic performance, and teacher feedback quality directly strengthens or erodes that conviction.
Grade caps (modeled after Harvard's approach) fail to address the root question of what a grade measures and simply redistribute grades without clarifying the student-teacher contribution split.

Students arrive with either task-mastery or ego-protection motivational orientations (Covington, 1984), and these are among the most consequential inputs a teacher inherits -- ones good instruction can shift but not ignore.
quotes: When a student walks into a classroom for the first time, she carries a grade with her. This is not the grade she will eventually earn, but the one she is already likely to earn. I'm not arguing for a mechanistic determinism that should force teachers to throw up their arms in defeat.

The Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) project, the most rigorous large-scale study of teaching effectiveness conducted in American K-12 education, built its methodology around a single, uncomfortable fact. Teachers have very different collections of students in every class they teach. Without controlling for what students bring to the classroom, which MET does by considering incoming test scores, any measure of teaching effectiveness is confounded from the start.

Students also bring motivational orientations that are deeply influenced by teacher practices. As Covington (1984) distinguished, learners arrive with either task-mastery goals or ego-protection goals.
